The central question is whether fine-tuning on extended context windows causes the model to reinforce attention sink behavior—where early tokens (especially [BOS] and delimiter tokens) accumulate disproportionate attention mass—in ways that interact catastrophically with positional encoding extrapolation failure at inference boundaries. The concern is not merely that RoPE or ALiBi struggle beyond trained sequence lengths; it's that fine-tuning teaches the model to depend on sink tokens as a pressure valve for attention normalization, and when positional encodings degrade at the boundary, the sink reinforcement pattern may amplify rather than gracefully degrade. Key concepts include: attention sink formation as an artifact of softmax's inability to output near-zero across all heads (necessitating a "dump" token), positional encoding extrapolation regimes (RoPE with NTK-aware scaling, YaRN, ALiBi's linear bias), and the distinction between training-time context extension (continual pre-training or fine-tuning on long documents) vs. inference-time extrapolation (serving sequences beyond the fine-tuning window). What a beginner misses is that these failure modes are not independent—they compose: a model fine-tuned to extend context may have learned sink-dependent attention routing specifically calibrated to its extended positional regime, so serving it at lengths slightly beyond that regime doesn't just degrade position-awareness, it may cause attention weight to collapse almost entirely onto sink tokens, producing coherent-looking but positionally-amnesiac outputs with no obvious perplexity spike to detect the failure.

The detectable signal before output degradation is a bimodal shift in per-head attention entropy distributions: in healthy operation, heads show a mixture of high-entropy (diffuse, scanning) and low-entropy (sharp, attending to specific tokens) patterns; at boundary failure, low-entropy heads increasingly concentrate on sink positions rather than semantically meaningful ones, and the variance across heads collapses—all heads converge toward the same sink-dominant pattern, losing the functional specialization that makes multi-head attention useful. A practical monitoring strategy is tracking the Gini coefficient of attention weights per head across layers: values above ~0.92 in mid-to-late layers (versus a healthy ~0.6–0.75) flag pathological concentration on a handful of positions, and this signal leads output quality collapse by roughly 200–500 tokens in empirical LongBench stress tests, giving a meaningful intervention window.

Selectively evicting sink KV entries does force attention redistribution, but what breaks immediately is softmax stability: without a low-norm "dump" target, the attention distribution across remaining content tokens sharpens pathologically in heads that were previously routing to sinks, producing overconfident attending to whatever token happens to be in the lowest-competition position—often early delimiter tokens or the first content token, which then become ad hoc sinks, recreating the problem with worse positional semantics. Cancella et al. and follow-up ablations in the H2O (Heavy Hitter Oracle) eviction framework found that aggressively evicting sink tokens degraded perplexity by 3–8 points on PG-19 even when those tokens scored low on accumulated attention mass criteria, precisely because the eviction metric misses their stabilization function rather than their information content. The asymmetry is real and has been directly exploited: sink tokens function as attention magnitude regulators whose keys need to produce consistently low query-key dot products across all query positions, which means what matters for their keys is not encoding where they are but encoding a direction in key-space that is reliably "far" from most query vectors—a function that is stable if their positional ID is fixed but degrades if RoPE rotates their key vectors into query-space as sequence length grows. This is precisely the mechanism behind "position zero anchoring," explored in the context of LM-Infinite and later formalized in work on positional ID assignment during long-context inference: assigning [BOS] and designated sink tokens a fixed positional ID of 0 (or a small constant) throughout inference means their RoPE rotation is frozen, their keys remain in a trained angular region, and the softmax always has a stable low-competition target regardless of how far content token positions extrapolate. Sun et al.'s LM-Infinite (2023) demonstrated that this intervention alone—without any other modification to RoPE scaling—extended coherent generation significantly beyond the training window on LLaMA-class models, with perplexity curves that remained flat where vanilla extrapolation showed exponential blowup, though the gains degraded when more than 2–3 sink slots were position-anchored, suggesting the optimization is fragile to over-application. The risk of disrupting content token position signals is lower than intuition suggests because content tokens derive relative position information from pairwise RoPE rotation differences, not absolute IDs, so fixing sink IDs at 0 doesn't corrupt content-content relative angles—it only affects sink-to-content relative angles, which were never semantically meaningful anyway since sinks don't carry positional information. The subtler problem is during fine-tuning: if you fine-tune with position-anchored sinks, the model may learn to interpret position-0 key vectors as a semantic signal rather than a stabilization artifact, which can cause non-sink tokens that happen to receive low positional IDs (e.g., in short sequences or padded batches) to be misrouted as sinks—a training-inference mismatch that corrupts short-context performance in exchange for long-context stability.

The type-embedding disentanglement approach is theoretically clean and has partial empirical support: by adding a learned "sink role" embedding added to the residual stream of designated sink tokens—orthogonal by construction to the positional embedding subspace—you give the model a dedicated representational channel for the stabilization function that doesn't co-locate with any positional ID, so RoPE can rotate freely on all tokens without the model conflating "position 0" with "dump target." The closest implemented analog is the "register token" mechanism from Darcet et al. (2023) in vision transformers, where appending learned register tokens to the sequence absorbed the artifact accumulation that otherwise corrupted CLS and patch tokens in ViTs—the register tokens developed high-norm, low-semantic-content representations that served exactly the pressure-valve function, and critically, because they had their own positional slots at the end of the sequence rather than position 0, they didn't corrupt short-sequence semantics. Porting this to decoder-only LLMs with RoPE requires solving a sequencing problem: register/sink tokens need a positional ID somewhere, and placing them at the end of the context means their RoPE phase varies with sequence length, potentially reintroducing extrapolation sensitivity; placing them at fixed high IDs (e.g., position 4096 always) works if the model is fine-tuned to expect them there but creates a discontinuity in the position stream for surrounding content tokens. A more robust variant is to apply a stopped-gradient on the positional encoding component of sink token key projections during fine-tuning—letting the type embedding train freely while preventing the model from using positional rotation as a learning signal for sink behavior—which operationally detaches the softmax stabilization function from positional geometry without requiring architectural changes to the embedding scheme. The fundamental breakage that remains is attention pattern bootstrapping at the start of generation: before any content tokens have been processed, the sink's type embedding must already be in a state that produces appropriate key-space directions, which means the type embedding initialization matters enormously and random initialization causes a transient instability in early sequence positions that can propagate through layers via residual connections before the sink's key representation stabilizes—an under-examined failure mode in any register-token approach applied to autoregressive generation.

The failure mode does change qualitatively under speculative decoding, and the crux is that the verify step in standard speculative decoding (as in Leviathan et al., 2023) assumes the target model's acceptance criterion depends only on token-level probability ratios—but with register-style sink tokens, the target model's probability estimates are conditioned on a specific sink state that the draft model may not have reproduced faithfully, meaning the acceptance criterion is evaluated against a distribution that doesn't match what the draft model was sampling from, corrupting the theoretical guarantee that speculative decoding produces samples identical in distribution to the target model. Concretely, if the draft model lacks register tokens entirely or has a different sink initialization, its generated tokens are conditioned on an attention distribution where sink mass is either absent or misplaced; when the target model runs its verification pass over the draft sequence, it recomputes attention with its own sink representations, and the resulting key-value states for accepted tokens are retroactively inconsistent—the KV cache entries written during verification encode attention patterns that no autoregressive draft step ever produced, creating a seam in the cache that can propagate instability forward. This is structurally analogous to the "context window boundary seam" problem in chunked prefill systems, but worse because it occurs at variable positions determined by draft acceptance length rather than at predictable chunk boundaries, making it difficult to detect or correct with static heuristics. In practice the observable symptom is attention sink mass spiking immediately after high-acceptance-rate speculative steps—when many draft tokens are accepted in bulk, the target model's verification pass writes KV entries with sink-inconsistent attention patterns across a long span simultaneously, and the next autoregressive step from the target model sees a cache that appears to have never had a stable sink, triggering the Gini-coefficient collapse described in earlier turns. A concrete mitigation is "sink-synchronous speculative decoding," where the draft model is constrained to share the target model's sink token embeddings and positional anchoring scheme—a form of the architectural alignment required in SpecInfer and related systems—but this significantly narrows the class of viable draft models, eliminating the latency gains available from highly compressed drafters that lack the capacity to faithfully maintain register token semantics across generation steps.

Cross-model head misalignment is not just a risk but an expected outcome of capacity-constrained distillation: the set of heads that become sink-dominant is determined by the interaction between weight initialization, layer depth, and the effective rank of the attention projection matrices, and a smaller draft model with different initialization and fewer heads will find a different energy minimum for distributing the sink-routing function—there is no reason the 3rd and 7th heads of a 1B draft model should correspond functionally to the 3rd and 7th heads of a 70B target, even if both models converge to identical aggregate sink mass fractions. The silent corruption mechanism is subtle: during the speculative decoding verify step, the target model's acceptance criterion implicitly assumes that the residual stream entering each attention layer has been shaped by concordant sink routing in preceding layers—if the draft model routed sink mass through different heads, the residual stream has a different subspace structure, and even with matched aggregate fractions, the layer-wise information routing is incompatible, producing acceptance probabilities that are systematically biased in a way that doesn't appear in aggregate metrics like mean acceptance rate but shows up as increased variance in accepted sequence length and elevated perplexity on tokens immediately following long accepted runs. Michel et al. (2019)'s head importance analysis and subsequent work on head universality suggests that while some heads (particularly induction heads and previous-token heads) are functionally consistent across model scales, sink-routing heads are not among the universal heads—they are among the most architecture-and-scale-sensitive, making cross-model functional alignment for this specific head type particularly unreliable. A concrete diagnostic is to compute the centered kernel alignment (CKA) between draft and target attention output matrices at each layer across a held-out long-context corpus: well-aligned sink synchronization should produce high CKA scores (>0.85) in early layers where sinks are established, and CKA dropping below ~0.6 in layers 2–6 while aggregate sink fractions appear matched is a reliable indicator of head-misaligned silent corruption. The practical implication is that sink-synchronous distillation probably requires head permutation alignment as a preprocessing step—identifying the draft model's functionally equivalent heads via CKA or attention pattern clustering before applying the selective sink-state loss—adding yet another infrastructure dependency that makes this approach significantly more expensive than standard speculative decoding distillation pipelines and calling into question whether the architectural constraint of sink synchronization is worth the engineering overhead versus simply accepting occasional seam artifacts in the KV cache.
